lesson.title: Reading numbers: units and scales
lesson.subtitle: Units, eye level and fair comparisons

video.title: Reading numbers: units and scales
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Salma’s maths classroom. Two pupils stand by a wall thermometer, each holding up a slate: one shows 30, the other 86. Classmates lean in from both sides. Salma folds her arms and raises an eyebrow at the camera, half smiling.
scenes.animation: Slates pop up one after the other; quick push-in on Salma’s raised eyebrow.
scenes.narration: Same thermometer, same minute. Huda writes thirty. Karim writes eighty-six. And they’re both convinced they’re right. Hmm. Maybe they are.
scenes.sound: Classroom chatter; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated secondary maths teacher, ink outlines. Numbers on the slates are fine; no other text or logos.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the IoT track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: reading numbers — units, scales, and how to compare readings fairly.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: Close-up of the wall thermometer: two scales, one on each side of the red liquid column. A teal line runs straight across from the top of the liquid to 30 on the left scale and 86 on the right.
scenes.animation: Camera slides up the column; the teal line draws across in 600 ms.
scenes.narration: Look closer: this thermometer has two scales. Thirty degrees Celsius on one side sits beside eighty-six degrees Fahrenheit on the other. Both pupils read correctly — they just didn’t write the unit.
scenes.vids: Generic dual-scale thermometer with no brand marks. Add the unit labels as text overlays, not baked into the art.

scenes.visual: Three cards pop up: a thermometer with a small degree circle, a raindrop over a ruler, a half-full battery beside a pie chart. A loose number floats in, wobbles between the cards, then snaps onto one of them.
scenes.animation: Cards pop 250 ms apart; the floating number wobbles, then snaps into place.
scenes.narration: A unit tells you what a number measures. Degrees Celsius for temperature. Millimetres for rainfall. Percent — out of a hundred — for things like battery level or how damp the air is. A number without its unit is only half a reading.
scenes.vids: Show units as text overlays so they can be translated. Hold all three cards for 3 seconds.

scenes.visual: Clean card on white with the IoT track chip. Four icons in a row — a number box, a unit tag, a clock and a map pin — joined by plus signs.
scenes.animation: Icons pop left to right, 200 ms apart.
scenes.narration: So here’s the rule. Every reading has four parts: the number, the unit, the time and the place. “Twenty-eight degrees Celsius, 8 am, shady wall by the door.”
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A busy border market. A trader holds up a bunch of tomatoes and calls out a price; his speech bubble shows two different banknote shapes with a question mark between them. A shopper tilts her head, unsure.
scenes.animation: Bubble pops; the two banknote shapes swap places twice.
scenes.narration: It’s like a price in a border market. “It’s two hundred.” Two hundred what — naira or CFA francs? A number without a unit is a price without a currency.
scenes.vids: Generic banknote shapes in flat colours; no real notes, flags or currency symbols. Lively, respectful market scene.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah Rahman pops in at her university office, holding a student’s notebook open to a weather log with one short line. Three answer cards drop in: a unit tag with a clock, a check mark, a name badge.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! My student’s weather log says just “Rain: fifteen.” Can we compare that with next week? What’s missing?
scenes.sound: Three gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The unit-and-clock card gets a blue check badge. The log line grows: the number gains a unit tag, then a small clock and a calendar icon slide in beside it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: The unit and the time. Fifteen millimetres? Since when — this morning, or all week? Add “mm” and “since 8 am yesterday”, and the number becomes useful.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: A big thermometer scale fills the screen, from 20 to 30 with five equal steps between. The steps light up one by one in teal. Then an eye slides up and down beside the liquid top until a teal sight line levels out.
scenes.animation: Steps light 200 ms apart; the eye glides, then settles level with a small check pop.
scenes.narration: Now, reading a scale. First, find what each small step is worth: five steps between 20 and 30 means each step is 2. Then bring your eye level with the top of the liquid. From above or below, the reading looks higher or lower than it is.
scenes.vids: Keep the scale large and simple so it reads on a small phone screen. Numbers on the scale only.

scenes.visual: Two thermometer cards side by side. Left: shade, a low dawn sun, liquid low. Right: full midday sun beating down, liquid high. A large question mark hangs between them, then the sun on the right card pulses.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in from both sides; the question mark drops in; the sun pulses twice.
scenes.narration: Last, compare like with like. Monday, 7 am, in the shade: 24 degrees. Tuesday, 2 pm, in full sun: 35. Was Tuesday hotter? We can’t tell. The time and place changed — and sun on a thermometer heats it directly, so it reads high.
scenes.sound: Light ‘swish’ as the cards slide in.
scenes.vids: Show the day names as text overlays. Keep both cards on screen for at least 4 seconds.

scenes.visual: Salma holds up two pairs of thermometer cards. Pair one: both in the same shade at 8 am. Pair two: one in shade at 8 am, one in sun at noon. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Which pair is a fair comparison? Two readings at 8 am in the same shady spot — or one at 8 am in shade and one at noon in the sun?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight the first pair.

scenes.visual: Pair one gets the check badge. Then four summary cards line up: a number box with a unit tag, an eye with a level line, a clock with a map pin, an equals sign between two matching thermometers.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The same time, the same shady spot — that’s fair. Remember: number plus unit, eye level, time and place, and compare like with like.
scenes.vids: Hold the four cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Salma’s classroom. A thermometer hangs on a shady wall at pupils’ eye height. A pupil reads it, eyes level, and writes in a class log pinned beside it while a classmate checks. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Build a rain gauge’.
scenes.animation: Pencil writes a short line; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: hang a thermometer in the shade. Each morning at the same time, a different pupil reads it at eye level and writes the number, the unit, the time and the place. No thermometer? Draw a big scale on the board and practise.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: A weather log says just “Rain: 15”. What is missing?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — “15 mm since 8 am yesterday” can be checked and compared. “15” alone can’t.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — without a unit and a time, nobody knows if it’s 15 mm in a day or in a week.

checkpoints.prompt: Which pair of readings is a fair comparison?

options.text: Both at 8 am in the same shady spot
8 am in shade and noon in the sun

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — same time, same place, same unit. Now a difference is more likely to come from the weather.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the time and the sun both changed, so you can’t tell what caused the difference.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3-minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Reading numbers: units and scales”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a teal (#14b8a6) track accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Ms Salma Haddad, a secondary maths teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: two pupils read 30 and 86 on one thermometer; why every reading needs a unit; the four parts of a reading; the border-market price analogy; a quiz pause; reading a scale at eye level; comparing like with like; a second quiz pause; recap; end with a daily class thermometer log. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
